description: Hey! We’re two Systems Engineering students, one developer and one data engineer, focused on building robust software, scalable pipelines, and high-impact data solutions. With backend development, system architecture, and data engineering fully covered, we’re looking for teammates skilled in UI/UX design, Front-End, or Product/Pitching to build a solid, competitive MVP together
summary:
The Eye of Sauron is an interactive web application and open-source data pipeline that unifies 25 years of satellite active-fire data from NASA’s MODIS (1 km resolution, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m resolution, since 2012) sensors into a single, consistent historical record.
   Because VIIRS detects several times more hotspots over the same fires than MODIS, raw combined datasets create a false artificial jump in burning activity in 2012. We solved this by calibrating a spatial scaling factor ($k$) per H3 hexagon (~36 km²) to translate VIIRS detections into standardized "MODIS units," explicitly tracking satellite coverage so missing downloads are never mistaken for zero fire, and assigning every detection a confirmation reliability index.  
   Accessible via an interactive burning activity calendar, anomaly explorer, multi-scale H3 map, and NASA POWER weather overlays, this tool enables scientists, emergency responders, and land managers to accurately identify seasonal fire anomalies and long-term climate trends without sensor-transition bias.
details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?

The Eye of Sauron is an interactive web application and open-source data lakehouse that unifies over 12.4 million active-fire detections (2000–2025) from NASA’s MODIS (1 km resolution) and VIIRS (375 m resolution) sensors into a single, continuous historical record.

Because VIIRS is significantly more sensitive and detects ~3.3× to 5.6× more hotspots over the same fires than MODIS, simply concatenating raw datasets creates a massive artificial jump in burning activity in 2012. In a test zone in Zambia (August 2019), raw VIIRS counted 6.6 times as many hotspots as MODIS (168,649 vs. 25,437), whereas after our harmonization pipeline, the two sensors agree within 10% (23,331 vs. 21,930) with zero step-change across the 2012 transition.

MODIS (~1 km) vs. VIIRS (~375 m) thermal sensitivity. VIIRS resolves smaller and cooler sub-pixel combustion fronts below MODIS's detection threshold, creating the artificial 2012 jump in raw combined records.

To achieve seamless cross-sensor continuity, our pipeline executes a four-stage data harmonization workflow:

Stage 1: Sensor Cleaning & Physical Normalization

Before comparing sensors, we remove systematic geometric artifacts in MODIS:

  • Bow-Tie Scan-Edge Deduplication: At the swath edge, consecutive MODIS scans overlap and double-count the same fire. By rotating each satellite pass into its along-track / along-scan coordinate frame (using orbital inclination 98.2°), we merge duplicate detections within 0.5 pixels in both directions—eliminating 8.1% to 8.8% of false daytime MODIS detections.
  • Pixel-Size FRP Correction & Noise Filtering: MODIS Fire Radiative Power (FRP) is normalized for scan-angle pixel stretching using empirically fitted factors (1.00 for < 1.2 km, 1.13 for 1.2–1.6 km, 1.15 for 1.6–2.2 km, and 1.26 for ≥ 2.2 km), reducing raw MODIS FRP edge bias by 26–29%. Low-confidence noise (MODIS < 30, VIIRS "low") and static industrial/volcanic heat sources are excluded.
Stage 2: Empirical Benchmarking of FRP vs. Harmonized Counts

Across 54,159 matched Aqua–S-NPP pixel pairs (≤ 30 min apart) and multi-year regional benchmarks (Paraná Delta, Iberá Wetlands, and Zambia), we quantified how sensor agreement behaves across spatial scales:

  • Single Pixel Footprint (≤ 30 min): Log-log correlation r = 0.59, multiplicative spread ×/÷ 2.6, median MODIS/VIIRS ratio 1.48.
  • 5 km Grid Cells (≤ 5 min, near-nadir): Log-log correlation r = 0.76, spread ×/÷ 1.8, median ratio ~1.01.
  • 25 km Grid Cells (≤ 3 min, near-nadir, ≥ 20 MW): Log-log correlation reaches r = 0.85 (spread ×/÷ 1.5), matching the physical ceiling observed between two identical MODIS sensors (Terra vs. Aqua).

Per-pixel vs. spatially aggregated FRP agreement. Individual pixel FRP shows high variance (r = 0.59) due to overpass timing and view angle, whereas spatial aggregation restores strong physical proportionality (r up to 0.85).

Because per-pixel FRP hits a natural physical correlation ceiling and sensitivity thresholds vary with view angle, our production pipeline combines spatially calibrated detection counts (expressed in standardized "MODIS units") alongside aggregated physical FRP (in megawatts). This architecture is sensor-agnostic and ready to onboard newer missions (NOAA-20, NOAA-21, and future thermal constellations) without breaking historical continuity.

Stage 3: Hierarchical Spatial Calibration (k) with Empirical Shrinkage

Using months where both MODIS and VIIRS S-NPP had verified 100% download coverage (2013–2025), we compute the VIIRS/MODIS scaling ratio (k = VIIRS / MODIS) across an H3 hexagonal hierarchy (Global → r2 → r4 → r6, ~36 km²). Each cell’s log(k) is shrunk toward its parent region weighted by sample size w = n / (n + 100). Out-of-sample cross-validation across alternate years proves hierarchical shrinkage outperforms both a single global factor and unregularized local cells:

  • Single Global k: Cross-validated RMSE = 0.76 (counts) and 0.79 (FRP) — too coarse for diverse ecosystems.
  • Unregularized H3 r6 Cell Alone: Cross-validated RMSE = 0.59 (counts) and 0.89 (FRP) — overfits noise in low-fire regions.
  • Hierarchical Shrinkage (Global → r6): Cross-validated RMSE drops to 0.42 (counts) and 0.63 (FRP) — preserving local precision in fire-prone zones while stabilizing quiet regions.

Out-of-sample splice validation on 2012–2014 (fitting k strictly on 2015–2025) confirms no detectable jump across the 2012 MODIS-to-VIIRS transition.

Stage 4: Explicit Coverage Tracking & Detection Reliability Index
  • Honest Data Gaps (fct_area_coverage_monthly): Active-fire tables only record rows where heat was detected, making missing downloads look identical to zero-fire days. Our lakehouse explicitly tracks every download window—including empty header-only files—ensuring unmonitored periods appear as transparent data gaps rather than false zeros.
  • Confirmation Reliability Index: Using spatio-temporal persistence (neighboring detections within 1.5 km and 1–36 h), sensor confidence, and log(FRP), a calibrated logistic model assigns every hotspot a probability of independent cross-satellite confirmation (validated out-of-fold AUC = 0.730 for VIIRS and 0.664 for MODIS).

Detection confidence, persistence, and spatial density. Combining sensor confidence with spatio-temporal persistence distinguishes sustained burns from transient single-pass anomalies.

2. Web Application Features & User Experience

Through the live interface (http://190.15.198.99:30000/), users can inspect pre-loaded regions or draw custom polygons to explore:

  • Burning Activity Calendar: A 25-year month-by-year heatmap with three instant modes: Raw, Harmonized (continuous series in MODIS units), and Anomaly (comparing any month against its multi-year historical median using distribution percentiles p10–p90 computed strictly over fully observed months).
  • Multi-Scale H3 Hexagonal Map & Time Slider: Dynamic hexagonal grids colored by normalized detection density (detections per 1,000 km² per day) paired with a day-by-day animation slider, NASA GIBS true-color satellite imagery, and SRTM terrain contour lines.
  • MODIS | VIIRS Comparison Curtain: An interactive split-screen swipe tool to inspect both sensors side-by-side in raw or harmonized units.
  • Hexagon History & Fire Weather Context: Clicking any hexagon opens its multi-decade activity chart, per-sensor Reliability Index report, and surrounding NASA POWER meteorological conditions (temperature, precipitation, wind, relative humidity, and vapor pressure deficit) displayed as non-intrusive radial icons.

3. Benefits, Intended Impact & Creativity

  • Scientific Continuity: Bridges the 25-year MODIS era (nearing decommissioning) with the VIIRS constellation (S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21) so climate scientists can analyze multi-decadal fire trends and El Niño droughts without sensor-transition bias.
  • Operational Decision Support: Gives emergency managers and conservation teams near-real-time (NRT) hotspots contextualized against 25 years of local historical baselines and live fire weather.
  • Creative Engineering: Instead of forcing brittle pixel-by-pixel matching or hiding uncertainty, we solved the problem at the data-architecture level—combining hierarchical empirical Bayes shrinkage on H3 grids, explicit empty-window coverage tracking, and non-intrusive radial weather icons around active fire cells.

4. Tools, Coding Languages & Software Stack

  • Data Engineering & ETL: Python, Apache Airflow, dlt (data load tool) for incremental NASA FIRMS (SP/NRT) and NASA POWER ingestion, and dbt (orchestrated via Astronomer Cosmos) for incremental SQL transformations and 50+ automated data quality contracts.
  • Storage & Spatial Analytics: DuckLake (open Parquet lakehouse with SQLite catalog) queried via DuckDB with spatial and h3 extensions.
  • Backend & Frontend: FastAPI (Python) REST API serving a Vue.js web application built with MapLibre GL, NASA GIBS WMTS tiles, and OpenStreetMap/SRTM layers.
